title_options: How A Spinning Motor In You Makes Energy ⚙️

share.myth: Cells make energy molecules by simple chemistry, with no moving parts.
share.truth: In ATP synthase, a rotating shaft squeezes each of three catalytic sites through open, loose and tight shapes, so every full turn makes three ATP (Boyer 1997, Annual Review of Biochemistry; Watt et al. 2010, PNAS).
share.line: Every turn of the tiny turbine in your cells squeezes out three ATP, about a hundred turns a second.

facts: Boyer PD 1997, Annu Rev Biochem 66:717: binding change mechanism; each catalytic beta site cycles through open, loose and tight states as the asymmetric central stalk rotates.
Watt IN et al. 2010, PNAS 107:16823: each 360 degree rotation makes 3 ATP; about 100 rotations per second.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1997: Paul D. Boyer and John E. Walker, for the enzymatic mechanism of ATP synthesis (shared with Jens C. Skou).
description: A crooked shaft turning inside ATP synthase squeezes three working parts into new shapes, and every turn makes three ATP. Chapter 6 of our book The Tiny Turbine That Powers Your Body. #shorts #biology #science #biochemistry
sources: Boyer 1997, Annual Review of Biochemistry 66:717 (binding change); Watt et al. 2010, PNAS 107:16823 (3 ATP per turn); Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1997.

scenes.narration: Every turn of this tiny turbine makes three molecules of ATP. Here's how.
The spinning ring turns a crooked shaft, inside a head of three working parts.
As the shaft turns, it squeezes each part into a new shape, one after another.
Open, to grab the pieces. Loose, to hold them.
Tight, to press them together into ATP. Then it opens and lets the ATP go.
That idea won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in nineteen ninety-seven.
Every turn of the tiny turbine in your cells squeezes out three ATP, about a hundred turns a second.
So what do you think happens to all those turbines when you start to run?
